title: Indian Shares Post Weekly Losses as Oil Surge and Rising Bond Yields Weigh on Sentiment
excerpt: Nifty and Sensex ended the week down 0.5-0.6% as Middle East crude price escalation and global bond market pressure kept investors cautious, though small-cap indices hit fresh 52-week highs.
body:
• Nifty 50 settled 0.08% higher at 24,252 on Friday while the Sensex closed flat at 77,540, but both indices posted weekly losses of 0.5% and 0.6% respectively.
  • Elevated crude oil prices driven by escalating Middle East conflict and rising global bond yields kept investors cautious throughout the week.
  • IT stocks fell 2.6% on U.S. inflation concerns, while private banks rose 1.3% after Goldman Sachs initiated coverage on 14 Indian lenders.
  • Small-cap indices bucked the trend, gaining 1.2% for the week and hitting fresh 52-week highs even as 12 of 16 major sectors logged losses.

Friday Close: Flat Finish Caps a Cautious Week

Indian equities ended the week on a muted note on Friday, with the Nifty 50 settling 0.08% higher at 24,252 and the BSE Sensex closing essentially flat at 77,540.83, according to Reuters.

The modest Friday uptick did little to offset a week of steady erosion. The Nifty fell 0.5% and the Sensex dropped 0.6% over the five sessions, as a combination of surging crude oil prices and spiking global bond yields squeezed risk appetite across emerging markets.

Other Asian peers also posted weekly losses, underscoring that the pressure was not India-specific.

Oil and Bonds: The Twin Headwinds

The week's dominant theme was crude oil. Brent prices climbed to near one-month highs as an escalating conflict in the Middle East reinforced inflation concerns globally. For India, which imports more than 80% of its crude requirements, higher oil prices directly threaten the current account deficit, corporate margins, and the Reserve Bank of India's inflation management.

"No market ever prices an ongoing conflict and its consequences fully. What we can see is that option skew shows participants paying for downside protection rather than taking a directional view."

— Rishabh Nahar, Partner and Fund Manager, Qode Advisors

Rising global bond yields compounded the problem. Stronger yields raise borrowing costs and curb overseas inflows into riskier assets like emerging market equities. While the U.S. Treasury's decision to double buyback sizes for long-duration debt on Thursday provided temporary relief — helping Indian markets snap a seven-session losing streak that day — the reprieve proved short-lived.

Sector Scorecard: Banks Up, IT and FMCG Down

Twelve of the 16 major sectors logged weekly losses. The most notable casualties were IT stocks, which fell 2.6% as concerns over persistent U.S. inflation raised questions about the pace of Fed rate cuts and client spending.

Private banks bucked the trend, rising 1.3% for the week. Kotak Mahindra Bank gained 3% and Axis Bank added 2.3%. The sector got a boost after Goldman Sachs initiated coverage on 14 Indian lenders, citing an improving earnings outlook, while Bernstein said banks could sustain healthy growth in FY2027 on robust liquidity and recovering credit growth.

The utilities sector was Friday's standout performer, gaining 1.27% on the session. Power Grid Corporation led large-cap gainers with a 3.73% jump, supported by positive sentiment around infrastructure spending.

FMCG was the biggest sectoral laggard on Friday, falling 0.83%, with Britannia Industries declining 3.5% amid concerns over margin pressures.

Stock Movers: Tata Motors Slides, Welspun Surges

Tata Motors was the biggest decliner in the Nifty 50 for the week, falling 5%. The stock has now lost 9.1% over six sessions after the company reported a decline in quarterly profit. Tata Motors also announced price hikes of up to 25,000 rupees ($261) on its cars and SUVs effective September.

On the positive side, Welspun Corp surged 15.3% on Friday after the pipe maker received a record $1.8 billion supply order from its U.S. manufacturing facility — the largest single order in the company's history.

Small Caps Shine Despite Broader Weakness

While large caps languished, small-cap indices gained 1.2% for the week. Multiple small-cap indices hit fresh 52-week highs on Friday, including the S&P BSE SmallCap Select Index, NIFTY SMALLCAP250, and NIFTY FREE SMALL 100. Mid-caps were essentially flat, declining just 0.1%.

Market breadth on Friday was nearly even, with 240 advances against 258 declines on the BSE500, indicating cautious but selective buying rather than broad-based positioning.

What to Watch Next Week

Crude oil prices remain the key variable. Any further escalation in the Middle East could push Brent higher and extend the selling pressure on Indian equities. The U.S. Treasury's bond buyback expansion has offered some breathing room, but its durability remains uncertain.

Investors will also watch for signals from the Reserve Bank of India on liquidity management and for any further corporate earnings surprises. The small-cap rally suggests domestic retail investors remain willing to buy on dips — but that confidence will be tested if oil-driven inflation fears intensify.
